about: Amaro Montenegro was created in Bologna in 1885 by Stanislao Cobianchi, who had turned down the priesthood his father intended for him and travelled widely collecting botanicals. He launched it from his own steam distillery as Elisir Lungavita, the “elixir of long life,” and in 1896 renamed it in honour of Princess Elena of Montenegro, who that year married the future King Vittorio Emanuele III. The poet Gabriele D’Annunzio later called it “the liqueur of virtues.” The company says the recipe has not changed since 1885.

Forty botanicals from four continents go into it, among them sweet and bitter orange peel, licorice root, nutmeg, vanilla and eucalyptus. They are sorted into groups, steeped for twenty to thirty days and distilled in 1,000-litre copper pot stills, yielding twelve “mother essences” that are blended into six aromatic notes. The seventh, called Il Premio, is a micro-distillate of five secret botanicals added at the very end, roughly one litre to every 15,000 litres of amaro. It is bottled at 23% alcohol.

Montenegro is one of Italy’s best-loved after-dinner bottles, and the critics agree: at the 2018 San Francisco World Spirits Competition it won a Double Gold and was named Best in Show Liqueur, and Falstaff scored it 91 points in 2022. Lighter in alcohol than most amari, it is poured neat, over ice, or with a twist of orange.
facts: Il Premio, a micro-distillate of five botanicals
title: Amaro Montenegro
